content: Ultrasound examinations conducted before 24 weeks of gestation can provide more precise pregnancy dating and enable earlier detection of fetal abnormalities. However, they may also lead to false reassurance. These scans are used to monitor fetal development or diagnose conditions in the unborn baby. This review evaluates the impact of routine or universal ultrasound performed before 24 weeks of gestation compared to selective or no ultrasound. The objective of this review was to determine the effects of routine ultrasound before 24 weeks as part of a screening program, compared to selective or no ultrasound, on outcomes such as early diagnosis of abnormal pregnancy location, termination for fetal congenital abnormalities, detection of multiple pregnancies, maternal outcomes, and later fetal complications. The review also separately assessed the effects of first-trimester (before 14 weeks) and second-trimester (14 to 24 weeks) ultrasounds. The search for relevant studies was conducted in Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) on August 11, 2020. Reference lists of retrieved studies were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, cluster-RCTs, and RCTs published in abstract form. Trials involving pregnant women who underwent routine or revealed ultrasound versus selective, no, or concealed ultrasound before 24 weeks of gestation were included. All studies were screened for scientific integrity and reliability. Two reviewers independently assessed the eligibility and risk of bias of the trials, extracted data, and verified the accuracy of the extracted data. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the certainty of evidence for each outcome. The review included data from 13 RCTs involving 85,265 women. Four trials were deemed to have a low risk of bias for sequence generation and allocation concealment, while two were assessed as having a high risk of bias. Due to the nature of the intervention, blinding of participants and care providers was not feasible. Most trials had low sample attrition, and outcome data were available for the majority of participants. Many of the included trials were conducted before trial registration and protocol publication became standard practice. First-Trimester Routine vs. Selective Ultrasound: Four studies involving 1,791 women from Australia, Canada, the UK, and the US were included. First-trimester scans likely reduce short-term maternal anxiety about pregnancy (risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65 to 0.99; moderate-certainty evidence). However, it is unclear if this reduction in anxiety is sustained over time. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effect of first-trimester scans on perinatal loss (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.73; 648 participants; one study; low-certainty evidence) or induction of labor for post-maturity (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.37; 1,474 participants; three studies; low-certainty evidence). The impact of routine first-trimester ultrasound on preterm birth before 34 weeks or termination of pregnancy for fetal abnormalities was not reported. Second-Trimester Routine vs. Selective Ultrasound: Seven studies involving 36,053 women from Finland, Norway, South Africa, Sweden, and the US were included. Second-trimester scans likely have little effect on perinatal loss (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.20; 17,918 participants; three studies; moderate-certainty evidence) or intrauterine fetal death (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.42; 29,584 participants; three studies; low-certainty evidence). Second-trimester scans may reduce the need for labor induction for post-maturity (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.73; 24,174 participants; six studies; low-certainty evidence), likely due to more accurate pregnancy dating. Routine second-trimester ultrasound may improve the detection of multiple pregnancies (RR 0.05, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.16; 274 participants; five studies; low-certainty evidence). Routine second-trimester ultrasound may increase the detection of major fetal abnormalities before 24 weeks (RR 3.45, 95% CI 1.67 to 7.12; 387 participants; two studies; low-certainty evidence) and likely increases the number of women opting for pregnancy termination due to major anomalies (RR 2.36, 95% CI 1.13 to 4.93; 26,893 participants; four studies; moderate-certainty evidence). Long-term follow-up of children exposed to prenatal scans did not show evidence of harm to their physical or intellectual development (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.34; 603 participants; one study; low-certainty evidence). The effect of routine second-trimester ultrasound on preterm birth before 34 weeks or maternal anxiety was not reported. Standard Care Plus Two Ultrasounds and Referral for Complications vs. Standard Care: One cluster-RCT involving 47,431 women from the Democratic Republic of Congo, Guatemala, Kenya, Pakistan, and Zambia was included. This trial also involved a co-intervention, including healthcare worker training and referral for complications, and was analyzed separately. Standard care plus two scans, along with training and referral for complications, likely has little effect on whether women with complications deliver in facilities equipped for cesarean sections (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.19; 11,680 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The intervention likely has little to no effect on the incidence of low birthweight (< 2,500 g) (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.13; 47,312 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain regarding the impact of this community intervention (including ultrasound) on maternal mortality (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.55; 46,768 participants; low-certainty evidence). Revealed vs. Concealed Ultrasound Results: One study involving 1,095 women from the UK was included. The evidence was very uncertain for all outcomes related to revealed versus concealed ultrasound results (very low-certainty evidence). Conclusions: Early ultrasound scans likely reduce short-term maternal anxiety. Later scans may reduce the need for labor induction for post-maturity, improve the detection of major fetal abnormalities, and increase the number of women opting for pregnancy termination due to these abnormalities. They may also reduce the number of undetected twin pregnancies. Neither firstnor second-trimester scans appear to significantly affect other important maternal or fetal outcomes. However, the review may underestimate the impact of modern ultrasound practices, as many trials were conducted during earlier stages of technological development, and many control participants also underwent scans. Additionally, the trials were underpowered to detect effects on other critical maternal or fetal outcomes.
